en: In the *Record of the Arising of Faith through Lotus Practice*, it is stated that the manifestation of the flying seer (fēiluán) for the purpose of transformation has existed for a long time. When the resonance of spiritual conditions produces a miraculous response, it reveals itself to people; yet the spirit itself cannot speak.
Let us speak by way of analogy. Let us speak by way of the objects in a person’s hands. If the spirit departs from the person, the *luan* [the writing brush] cannot be moved.
If the person departs from the spirit, the *luan* likewise cannot be moved. Yet, characters fall upon the sandboard as if flying, and their radiant energy radiates in all directions.
One must not gaze upon it closely; neither person nor object can maintain its autonomy. That this is not a mere fabrication is perfectly evident. Someone asked:
"Regarding the deity who descends through the spirit-medium (luán), does the deity employ the medium? Or is there actually a physical entity that employs the medium?

Little do they realize that between heaven and earth there is but a single vital energy (qì) filling all space. As for the spirit of the deity, on the grand scale it coils across the heavens and the earth; on a small scale, it is merely...
Entering into a mustard seed. As the Sūtra says: "The King of the Asuras, by exercising his supernormal powers, made the size of his body fill the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
yet he could hide that small form within a fiber of a lotus root. This was spoken with his own golden mouth by Śākyamuni Buddha; it is certainly not a false word.
Among the various deities of good and evil in the three realms, their merit and virtue vary in thickness, and their power varies in magnitude. [Their] pronouncements are...
Regarding the refined and the coarse: in general, that which exhorts toward good and punishes evil is orthodox; that which deludes the world and deceives the people is heterodox.
Once good and evil are distinguished, right and wrong are clearly adjudicated. What doubt can there be concerning [Seng]luan?

When the Bodhisattva Jingyun completed the *Record of Cultivating Faith through Lotus Practice* compiled by Chengzi, he requested a preface from me. I said: "In the past, the Sage of Xuan taught the world through the Six Classics;
though his Way was great, it was difficult to remedy the corruptions of the later ages. Our Buddha opened the gates of compassion and skillful means."

This Dharma gate consists of the four-character mantra, which universally benefits the boundless. Those of superior wisdom may, through mindfulness of the Buddha, clarify the mind and realize its nature, thereby attaining liberation from birth and death.
Those of middling and inferior capacities may, through mindfulness of the Buddha, turn toward goodness and ensure that they do not give rise to thoughts of committing evil.

Falling into the three miserable realms, our Buddha’s heart to save the world regards all beings—whether high or low, sharp or dull—with equal compassion, universally gathering them without exception.
Is this not a great Dharma gate for assisting the world and aiding the teachings? Alas!
Human hearts have become ever more deeply mired; only this single phrase of Amitābha remains capable of salvation. If this path were once closed, there would be no other [means].

Regarding the Dharma by which sentient beings may be rescued and delivered, I exhort all beings: you should recite the name of Amitābha early and often. There are three methods for the practice of Buddha-recitation:
mental recitation, oral recitation, and physical recitation. Mental recitation is supreme; physical recitation is next; and oral recitation is inferior to those.
A person who practices Buddha-recitation must first clarify the mind. When the mind is clarified, the Buddha is within the mind; when the Buddha is in the mind, [liberation is attained].
Then one will not be separated from the Buddha for even a single moment. If one can truly remain inseparable for even a moment, then even within dreams and sleep, the Buddha will be present;
even within dreams and sleep, the Buddha being present means the spirit has already roamed through the Buddha-lands.

It is like the dream of Huangdi entering Huaxu, which was precisely the spirit roaming through the Pure Land. If one can achieve this while alive, why worry that one will not be reborn there after death? As for people today...

Regarding the recitation of the Buddha's name: though the lips may chant many times, the spirit’s mindfulness is meager. For the most part, one is distracted by various desires; the mouth recites while the mind is in turmoil.
The appearance is that of the Buddha, yet the spirit is not. How can this be called "reciting the Buddha's name"? I observe the sentient beings' wisdom and virtuous marks.
Who is not like the Tathāgata? At birth, one is initially without knowledge, a state of pure and undifferentiated heavenly principle (*tianli*). A mind and nature such as this is precisely Amitābha.

If one remains thus for the rest of one’s life, who cannot attain rebirth in the Pure Land? Who cannot achieve Buddhahood? As the Sūtra says: "When a single Buddha dwells within the heart, all demons completely retreat.
With no obstacles during life, at the end of one's life, one attains rebirth. This is the constant law of principle. There is none.
How truly strange it is! Alas, how the private desires of sentient beings increasingly obscure their vision, leading them to greed, stinginess, deceit, and hypocrisy;

they act with craftiness and commit atrocities, creating hundreds of kinds of evil karma. Consequently, they cannot escape the three miserable realms and will inevitably enter the cycle of saṃsāra—this is truly lamentable.
This book reveals the methods for cultivating pure karma and the verified accounts of rebirth by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; it is like having a guide when traveling on a road.
It is like having a candle for one who has entered the darkness. Since you have come to know the excellence of *nien-fo*, do not let this life pass in vain.

A human body is difficult to obtain, and the Buddha-dharma is difficult to encounter; having already obtained it and encountered it, this is an opportunity that will not be met again for ten thousand kalpas.
Exert yourself and be cautious. This serves as the preface.

I once read the *Analects of Confucius*, and upon reaching the chapter on "Do not be arbitrary, do not be compulsive, do not be obstinate, and do not be self-centered," I sighed that [the mind] is formed by intention.
"I" and "I again" give rise to the will; objects of desire pull one along, cycling without end. Only Confucius completely severed the roots and stems;
his hidden intent accords with the great purport of Buddhism. Why say this? Formerly, the Bodhisattva Jue-ming-miao-xing said:
The sphere of mental activity exists; this is the mind of sentient beings' karma of birth and death. The mind is fundamentally without thought; thought arises following after perceptions.
These perceptions are illusory and false, causing one to transmigrate through birth and death, much like what Confucius called "private intent. Indeed, private intent and deluded thoughts—
Attachment to worldly passions arises entirely from mistakenly identifying the physical body as the self and clinging to it as such. Consequently, one creates various kinds of karma;
for the sake of this physical form, one seeks one's own benefit regardless of harming others and nourishes the body at the expense of causing great injury to living beings.

How could one know that the four elements will eventually decay and that the three miserable realms are unavoidable? The Buddha said that since beginningless time, sentient beings have mistaken a thief for their son and have stolen from themselves.

Household treasure! Alas, how can you be deluded by worldly toil and lose your true nature? If you can truly be without preconceived intent and without self, such that form is emptiness and emptiness is form, then the virtue of the mind will be perfectly complete.
Abiding in the world, you will become a sage who bestows grace; the light of your mind will shine universally.
Transcending the world constitutes the compassion of all Buddhas; Confucianism and Buddhism share this same source of the mind.
They are identical in this essential nature, and likewise identical in their meritorious practices. Master Cheng detested the dust of the mundane world, while Master Fa purified his Buddha-nature.

They reached a silent accord with my late father regarding pure cultivation. At times they would consult the *Chu sanzang jiji*. When [Cui] Qing grew weary of travel and returned to his native village, he recently looked up to the compassionate radiance of [the Master]. By...
Regarding these causes and conditions across two lifetimes, I have fortunately encountered a supreme spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).

I have been graced by the instruction of the precious teachings bestowed through mediumship by various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the years within this Dharma assembly, as well as the verses composed for the edification of fellow practitioners by various superior beings who have attained rebirth through mediumship.
Furthermore, I have humbly read the memorial written by Master Jing while in the Dharma assembly, which seeks to uproot the suffering of sentient beings throughout the great earth.
...the remainder. It is as if I were listening to shouts and blows; I often lament that the human heart is daily decaying, a state entirely brought about by pseudo-scholars and superficial gentlemen.
For farmers, artisans, merchants, and peddlers do not discourse on literature, and thus they dare not engage in reckless defiance;

yet, as the study of the Sages gradually perishes, those who read books fail to clarify the principles of nature and reason (*xingli*). Consequently, wild youths with sharp heads and keen faces disparage the precepts against killing and against lust.
This is erroneous and perverse; it even goes so far as to treat those who oppose the Triple Gem as heretics.
The Tripitaka states that slandering the True Dharma is equivalent to the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds.

Such cruelty and ignorance are truly the Pāpīyas of the Buddha-realm and the dregs of the Confucian community. This is the reason for the compilation of Master Jing’s "A Brief Discourse on Cause and Effect."

Master Jing, by virtue of his innate capacity for *prajñā*, attained still and profound realization of Gautama’s teaching. He was endowed with the faculties suited for the Perfect and Sudden [teachings], yet he opened the path of skillful means (*upāya*).
This is what is meant by "exhorting people through speech for a single lifetime, and exhorting people through writing for a hundred generations.
That his vows were vast and profound, ultimately bringing benefit and merit to humans and devas, is truly beyond words. Twenty years ago, Master Jing...
Having attained realization of the authentic transmission of the Elder He’s Pure Land Dharma Gate, he thereafter disregarded toil and hardship to establish a society and exhort others.
He personally drew blood from the tips of his ten fingers before the Buddha and made forty-eight vows.

He painted images of the two holy ones, Amitābha and Kṣitigarbha, and transcribed thirty-two sections of the inner scriptures, both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, which he enshrined within a seven-storied pagoda for veneration.

He performed cremations, constantly writing [sutras] for ten years. With such vast compassion, he sought to redeem his deceased parents and teachers from their transgressions so they might transcend to higher rebirths.
I have long forgotten the intentions of Master Jing; he universally ferried across both enemies and kin. His purity is truly beyond compare, beyond compare!
For decades, I have wandered like grains of sand in the Ganges, feeling ashamed that I have not fulfilled the aspirations of my predecessors.
Having received the guidance of my lord, I have had a fleeting vision of Amitābha;

thus, I have bathed myself in purity and respectfully composed this preface, hoping that all those in future generations who behold this collection will cleanse their hearts and purify their thoughts, and extensively give rise to bodhicitta—this is indeed the fundamental vow of our master Jinggong.
At this time...
Preface respectfully composed by Chen Muqing of Dongting, a junior student from the same prefecture, on the latter part of the Qinghe month in the year Wuzi,
the fourteenth year of the Guangxu era.
Śākyamuni dwelt in this world for forty-nine years, preaching immeasurable Dharma gates, all of which are fully detailed in the Dragon Canon (*Nāgārjuna-piṭaka*).
Among these, the single gate of Pure Land *nienfo* was established as a direct pointing to a supreme expedient for those sentient beings of the final age who lack strength;

by merely being able to maintain a single mind without distraction, one immediately enters the orthodox tradition of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching. Only those of superior wisdom and sharp faculties find it not difficult to have deep faith in this.
Yet it is said that the Chan practitioner who dwells in emptiness gives rise to doubt at every turn. Now that we have entered the Dharma-ending age (*mappō*), false views proliferate daily;

thus, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, out of compassion for sentient beings falling into ruin, relied upon the medium of a spirit-ravishing rhapsody (*luán*) to transform them and awaken those in delusion.
*Qixin lun* (The Awakening of Faith) is truly a compassionate vessel for saving the world and a staff-and-shout of the Buddha-dharma. This book was compiled by the Layman Yanchen.

Presented. The lay practitioner [Xue] Qixin has settled his mind in the realm of purity; his meritorious practice is profound and sincere. I have long admired his hidden cultivation and sought his instruction.

Consequently, he presented this compilation for my inspection. Having read it repeatedly, I see how it clarifies principle through concise matters, allowing one to investigate the profound through the shallow.
In truth, this is able to accord with the source of the mind and provoke deep reflection in people; it is the direct proclamation of the Golden Mouth, leaving no room for doubt. Someone might say:
"Manifesting through spirit-writing is a matter of establishing instruction through divine ways (*shendao*). Our Buddha takes cessation (*nirvāṇa*) as his primary principle;
how could he again engage in such devious tricks? I replied: "What you say is indeed correct. The reason I believe is that I believe in its underlying principle."

It is not that the matter is one of mere mud; rather, if one were merely to cling to historical facts and regard what is seen with one's own eyes as the truth, then we ordinary beings—who have never personally beheld the Buddha—would surely conclude that the Tripitaka and Twelve Divisions of Sūtras transmitted to China are all not the words of the Buddha.
Therefore, those who possess perfect penetration rely solely on principle. Once their faith in principle is firm, they view these [scriptures]...
It may be said that this book was spoken by the Buddha; yet it is not spoken by the Buddha. Nevertheless, there is nothing improper in regarding it as the Buddha’s teaching.

If one were to reject it simply because the words emerged from a spirit medium (ji), I do not know how such a thing could be justified. Having thus washed my hands in preparation, I have written this preface.
Preface respectfully inscribed by the Pure Land disciple Zhang Jingguan, having bathed in perfumed water, on the second day of the middle winter month in the year of Jiawu,
the twentieth year of the Guangxu era.
Zhao Luan is a fool who, in his youth, was ignorant of the Buddha-dharma. Having been moved by spirit-mediumship (ji-yu), he resolved to seek enlightenment.

For several decades he has practiced with diligence and has come to possess some understanding. Unable to bear the thought of casting it away like a worn-out broom, I have briefly set forth its general outline and placed it at the beginning of this work.

I have thus composed this preface. My family was registered in Hailang. During the Daoguang era, my late father successively accepted invitations from the Magistrate of Gaoyou Prefecture and the two Commandants of Fan and Wei.
Consequently, we moved our residence to Youzhou. During the Xianfeng era, when the Guangxi rebels caused turmoil in northern Jiangsu, the people of the prefecture fled in haste.
I too accompanied my mother to live among the rural villages, where I daily kept company with woodcutters and herdsmen.

I was unaware of the Buddha-dharma. One night, I dreamed that I was in a vast wilderness. I saw several dozen people, both monastics and laypeople, all kneeling on their right knees with palms joined, reciting the Buddha’s name.
A bhikṣu among them came forward and struck my shoulder, saying, "When the great kalpa arrives, do you still not know to recite the Buddha’s name?
Startled and alarmed, I woke up. Later, I went to the home of Zhang Jinmen to observe the spirit-writing séance (fúluán). One—
The Immortal descended and said, "The great kalpa has not yet ended; I am busy inspecting at the command of the Emperor.

At this, I suddenly recalled the words of the bhikṣu in my dream, and my heart throbbed with agitation. Privately I conjectured, unsure whether it was true or false, thinking to raise a hidden matter as a challenge.
Suddenly, the spirit-writing board called out my childhood name. I was then struck with alarm. You gave me that name, but Zhang did not know it.
He judged me, saying, "You possess profound latent roots from former lives. Why do you not swiftly sever worldly afflictions and turn your heart toward pure practice? I bowed in gratitude;
this was the beginning of my resolve for enlightenment. At that time, the miasma of banditry spread across the land, and the Imperial Commissioner of Education had long ceased his inspections.
I resolved to abandon Confucian studies and embrace Buddhism, serving Dharma Master Wuhua with close devotion morning and night, until I understood the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.
I alone, through the medium's words, was exhorted toward awakening. Thereafter, I invited the medium twice every month.
Whenever the discourse touched upon Buddhism, I recorded it as it occurred, eventually compiling them into a substantial volume. Previously, Elder Wuhé had established the Yongqing Nianfo Society;
after the Master passed away, I succeeded to his command and led the assembly. The medium changed the name to the "Wisdom Way-Place" (Zhìhuì Dàochǎng) and further stated:
"Your pure causes have not yet matured; practice mindfulness of the Buddha with patience. This altar shall sustain you for twenty years.
That year, an epidemic spread, leaving many physicians at their wits' end. King Hwa prescribed various remedies to save the world, and they were invariably effective.

Consequently, in addition to my mindfulness of the Buddha, I also engaged in the release of captive creatures, my resolve becoming even more firm. Furthermore, I received a command from the spirit medium to travel to the empty prisons.
Regarding the various repentance rites for bestowing alms, saving from suffering, and eliminating calamities, one should recite the Buddha’s name for seven days during each rite.

I urge you all that if you indeed recite the Buddha’s name with sincere devotion, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas shall surely come to your aid. All these judgments are fully detailed in the subsequent records.

Now, for those who cultivate the practice of Pure Land, the three characters of faith, aspiration, and practice are most difficult to make truly earnest. One’s daily cultivation must not be a mere matter of superficial effort; it requires a "dead heart" [a heart set on nothing else].
Regarding the practice of "Treading the Ground": at the moment of death, how can one achieve single-mindedness without distraction?
Master Lianchi said: "Faith, Vow, and Practice are the three provisions for the Pure Land. Once these provisions are complete, one will surely behold the Compassionate King. How profound these words!

Those who cultivate the Pure Land practice must by no means change their morning resolve for the evening or seek to shift from one path to another. It is simply necessary to take up a single item of daily practice and, from it—

From beginning to end, practice with single-minded faith. Faith is the mother of all merit; it nurtures all roots of goodness. Whatever vows one may make, they shall endure until the very limits of the future.

Even if the blade and saw were placed before one, one’s body and life might be sacrificed, yet this single thought of sincere devotion remains free from resentment or fear, without doubt or regret, never to be lost or regressed. This is the expedient method for the Pure Land.

This gate is called "Exiting the Three Realms Horizontally. It is not like "Exiting the Three Realms Vertically" through the practice of Chan meditation or the observance of the Vinaya, where one cannot achieve liberation in a single lifetime.
For example, consider a single bamboo stalk with thirty-three nodes: one who practices vertically must bite through each node in succession before finally penetrating to the very top;
one who practices horizontally is like boring a hole through the side and emerging from it directly. To the utmost...
It is swift and rapid. Among the Forty-eight Vows of Amitābha Buddha, it is said:
"If there be any sentient beings who call upon my name and yet are not born in my land, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment.

If a practitioner is willing to have faith and rely upon the Buddha’s vow, they will certainly transcend the three realms at the end of this present life. Although those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha in the world are many, the majority merely harbor expectations.
Among those who seek to make vows and dedicate their merit for the sake of present and future rewards, not even one or two in a hundred do so.
If one practices *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) in this manner, in what year will one behold Amitābha?

As for the deliverance of deceased ancestors and the guidance of beings back to Sukhāvatī, if one’s sincerity truly accords with the Dharma, the path of resonance and response will naturally manifest. Yet in the world, people treat Buddhist practice as child's play, and many burn [incense or paper money]...

Paper money and funeral offerings cause the deceased to cling to these forms and give rise to greed; thus, as before, they remain submerged and deluded within the five desires, making it difficult to escape the cycle of saṃsāra.

Their inverted ignorance and delusion are truly pitiable. Since my own parents passed away and I have felt the sorrow of the wind-blown tree, I have found no way to repay their boundless, profound kindness.
It was only later, upon reading the writings of Master Lianchi—the eighth patriarch—that I finally understood how one may seek to repay the debt of parental grace.

Nothing compares to the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha. By relying on the power of Amitābha to dedicate the deceased spirits toward liberation from suffering and rebirth in the Pure Land, this constitutes the ultimate filial piety.
One cannot count the instances of ancient sages who drew their own blood to transcribe the sutras. (Zhao Luan) Looking up to these former practitioners, his tears fell like rain.
Thus, before the Triple Gem, he prostrated himself and made a vow; subsequently, drawing blood from his fingers, he transcribed thirty Mahāyāna sutras.

[The text] consists of two volumes. He transcribed it continuously for ten years. On the day the task was completed, he constructed a seven-storied pagoda of silk brocade and offered it to the scripture.
He invited fellow practitioners of the Way to recite the Buddha’s name for seven days and nights, after which he cremated the manuscript.
He submerged the ashes in Zhuluo Lake at Mengcheng, on behalf of all sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu*—his parents, teachers, and elders throughout beginningless lifetimes, birth after birth.
Born [into this life], I repent and eliminate my karmic offenses. Relying upon this humble sincerity, may we together be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).

The spirit medium’s judgment states: "Drop by drop, drop by drop of blood, it shines through the seven-jeweled walls of the Western Paradise. Those of the Three Vehicles and the Seven Realms depart from Saṃsāra;
by virtue of your meritorious achievements, you shall transcend to the Pure Realm. This year I am sixty-six years old; my hair and beard are like frost, and my teeth are gradually falling out. From—
I know this illusory dwelling is difficult to inhabit for long. My past roots of purity are nearly complete;
of those I have known throughout my life, half already have their tomb-grass growing thick. In the autumn of the Jiawu year, having finished my Pure Land recitations, I sat alone by the lamp.
As the rain dripped from the wutong trees and the crickets wailed in lament, I sighed at how time flows like a stream and marveled that human life is but a dream. I took up my brush and wrote:

This is offered as an instruction for future generations. Having sifted through several fragments of old records by Master Luan preserved in my chest, and further appended a few of my own humble compositions, I have compiled them into six volumes entitled *The Record of the Arising of Faith in Lotus Cultivation*.
I have set aside the surplus from my frugal diet and clothing to commission the carving of these woodblocks.
As the ancients said: "In one lifetime, one may exhort others with the mouth; in a hundred lifetimes, one may exhort others with books. If this...
May the Dharma protected by the heavens be widely and far-reaching in its circulation, so that one may spontaneously evoke the sprouts of goodness and possess immeasurable faith.
This humble expression of my earnest concern is merely what I pray for and seek. Thus, I compose this verse: The Great Vows of Amitābha Buddha.

Exhaustively delivering all sentient beings without weariness, the people of this world deeply believe in and diligently practice [the teachings]. They shall swiftly realize the Lotus Land, holding the left-hand contract;

the flying phoenixes spread transformation with a heart of great compassion (*karuṇā*). With the sword of wisdom, they sever affliction and eliminate vexation throughout the past, present, and future, pervading all sentient beings within the three realms.
I now prick my own blood to transcribe this Golden Sutra, to offer in worship to the Compassionate King.
I pray that you will deign to look upon this. The seven-tiered pagoda is the radiance within one’s nature; the single phrase of Amitābha is recited from the heart.

May we be born together in Sukhāvatī and leave the wheel of suffering behind, so that my compassionate aspirations may be fulfilled and I shall no longer cling to the dust of the world. May all sentient beings develop true faith and universally turn their light [upon others];
do not again fall into folly and give rise to deluded views. Alas! The high talents and scholars of this world slander the Buddha-dharma, regarding that which transcends the world as...
They are called "fools. Yet how could they know that transcending the world is the foremost insight of a great man?
Master Chushi said: "Among ten billion people, only one or two understand. Thus we know that those whom others call fools are not actually fools;
rather, those who call them fools are themselves foolish, for they do not even recognize their own folly. How tragic!
Record of Arousing Faith in the Cultivation of the Lotus, respectfully composed by the sixty-six-year-old elder and disciple of the Pure Land school, Cheng Zhaoluan,
with hands washed in reverence, in the sixth month of the first winter of the Jiawu year of the Guangxu era.

*Record of the Arousing of Faith through Lotus Practice*, Scroll One.
Compiled by Cheng Zhao-luan of Hai-ling.
*Preserved Precious Instructions for the Lotus Land*, Part One.
Regarding the Great Strength Bodhisattva’s Jewel-like Instruction for Cultivating Pure Karma:
First, step with measured pace; then, hold fast to the single character. Next, from "one is not one" to "not one is one," one must leap with sovereign ease.
Whether moving or still, remain as suchness; whether hidden or manifest, leave no trace, shifting and interchanging at all times.

It should be so. Clarify the mind and awaken through illumination. When the "mother's face" turns over, you will immediately see and know for yourself. Body and mind both vanish; nature and Buddha are both forgotten.
Alertness and stillness are one; stillness and alertness are one. To know ice is water, and to know water is ice:
the myriad streams return to the source, becoming a single expanse of clarity. It is empty yet not empty, not empty yet empty. This is the foremost among states beyond grasping.
It is a single grasp. Proceeding in this manner, how could there be the calamity of falling into emptiness? There is naturally the fist that holds the hand.
These two characters, "holding the hand," are originally the cognitive perspective of the Two Vehicles. If one can always accord with sentient beings, it is a holding that is not holding.
To guard without guarding is to advance to a further level. To practice in accordance with the nature of awakening results in all things being perfect and sudden.
Knowing that habitual causes are illusory defilements, all phenomena are seen as empty. To give rise to two thoughts is to open wide the gates of obstruction;
to withdraw into a single thought is for all demons to vanish from sight. When thoughts arise, mist and smoke suddenly appear; when the mind is still, the ten directions are reflected therein.
Che. If one can let every drop return to its source, then naturally this will move that and that will respond to this.
You who cultivate the pure karma should listen with an empty mind.
This is the Precious Instruction of Bodhisattva Minghuavarada.

I was once among the Lotus Society of Master Yuan of Jin, where I practiced the method of seated meditation (*zuo chan*). For all who practice seated meditation, one must first settle into stillness and harmonize the breath.
Once the breath is balanced, one uses the eyes to observe the nose, and the nose to observe the mind.

Sitting with knees tucked in, neither leaning to the left nor to the right, one does not think of anything within the mind. The mindful heart is like water, entirely free of ripples, even if someone were present.
When others joke and laugh, although my ears hear them, my mind is not shaken by them; this is the beginning of sitting in meditation (*dhyāna*).
After sitting for several days, do not allow discursive thoughts (*vikalpa*) to arise. If one sits again for several days in this manner, discursive thoughts will naturally diminish;

this is the beginning of pacifying the mind and stabilizing the distracted. When not sitting in meditation, the mind can remain constantly settled; when sitting in meditation, the mind becomes even more...

It becomes easy and level. When the mind is level, the vital energy (*prāṇa*) harmonizes; when the vital energy harmonizes, the spirit (*śiva*) coalesces. After the spirit has coalesced, one adds the practice of *nien-fo* (reciting the Buddha’s name).

With every thought dwelling upon the heart, one immediately beholds the various sacred images. This causes the mind to become pure and the vital energy to be refreshed, leading to a sense of spontaneous joy as well as awe and reverence.
All worldly sentiments are entirely forgotten. At this time, one should continue to collect the mind and recite the Buddha’s name. If...
The moment a thought arises, in an instant all the extraordinary visions vanish; there is only my own body sitting upright here.

Upon descending from the seat and stepping outside, looking up and observing down, it is still nothing but a mass of turbid air—this is by no means the same as the scene of reciting the Buddha’s name within meditative concentration.
Therefore, he composed a verse: "Light and shadow flicker, about to rise and float; Sentient beings do not exist within heaven and earth."
The body of the Water-Crystal Tathāgata appears in its entirety; the veins and channels of the lotus are translucent and exquisite.

As for the practice of nianfo (buddha-recitation), whether it be mental recitation or verbal recitation, with sound or without sound, there is no need to be restrictive. In all cases, when the divine light is concentrated within, this is termed samādhi.
To attain this, one must listen to its sound with both ears, so that the spirit does not wander outward and delusive thoughts naturally recede.

As time passes—longer and longer—the light of the mind and the sound of the mind become a single, numinous mechanism. By perfuming the numinous with the numinous, one is able to invoke the Buddha. This is the secret method for transforming the bones:
sending the sound out through the mouth from within the light, and receiving the light back in through the ears from within the sound. By means of this majestic radiance...
Nourish your own mind and spirit. When the mind and spirit gather in perfect stillness, deluded thoughts will naturally vanish.

That people cannot become Buddhas is not because they lack anything; it is entirely because since beginningless time, the seeds of habitual tendencies have not been fully eradicated, and they have failed to cultivate their minds properly.
Thus, evil invades from within, using thought to draw forth the light, which enters and exits, repeatedly perfuming the consciousness until it is no longer capable of emerging.
It is not an entrance; there is neither interior nor exterior. After a long time, one attains great mastery, yet there is nothing that can be told to others.
O Samantamati Bodhisattva, I observe the sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age:
they are entangled and oppressed by emotional conditions, and their defilements and obscurations are difficult to eliminate. Though they may encounter Dharma gates, they do not seek them.
Though one exerts diligence and gains some slight awakening, one immediately claims to be capable;

thus, in a blur, a lifetime passes while remaining a transient guest, and for a long half-life, there is still no prospect of realizing the fruits of the path. Those who have received the Three Refuges turn their thoughts away from revering the Triple Gem.
Those who seek the five precepts will find it difficult to escape the five signs of decay in the long run.

If there are practitioners of true cultivation who seek the means to transcend the world, they should know that while reciting the Buddha’s name is easy, maintaining the mind of mindfulness is difficult; while verbal recitation is easy, stabilizing the mind is difficult. One must conceal one's faults with a sense of shame.
The arising of the mind is now manifest; yet within this manifestation, that which is hidden remains entirely hidden. Within that which is hidden, that which is manifest is not truly manifest.

One who can understand this principle will naturally find that the single thought-moment completely dissolves and all conditions become quiescent. It is not hidden and yet it is manifest; it is not manifest and yet it is hidden. It is not empty and yet it is empty;
it is empty and yet not empty. It is neither mind nor form; it is neither form nor emptiness. There is both existence and emptiness.
There are signs; having fully realized ultimate emptiness, the Dharma gates are immeasurable, and the wondrous lies within them. Sentient beings must apply themselves with diligence to attain this;

do not be like a common old man who speaks in vain. Thus he spoke in verse: "A single phrase of Amitābha penetrates all dharmas; It parts the turbid waters and brings one out from the cage of the mundane.
If you can recite Amitābha’s name to the depths, You are then a venerable one adorned for the Land of Ultimate Bliss. — Yuanlang (圓朗)
The power of the sound of the Dharma reaches its limit; the ear-vein’s illumination enters the heart. The numinous light intermingles and protects, encompassing heaven and earth.

Suddenly, one hears a single stroke of the bell from the western mountains: the Three Teachings return to their origin, which is emptiness. Life after life, one is liberated, and all conditions are penetrated.
To awaken to the fundamental source is true awakening; this single state of suchness is not easily encountered. The moon shines bright in the mid-heavens, pure and soundless;

beneath the water, the waves are clear as tree shadows stretch across them. If you wish for there to be no trace of shadow within the water, you must exhaustively bring forth the arising of all obscurations and defilements.
Zen practice and the recitation of the Buddha’s name share the same principle: it requires only that the mind be utterly empty. A single point remains unilluminated.
The Māra disturbs himself; the four modes of birth are liberated, realizing the primordial penetration. Ten thousand mountains with steep cliffs are illuminated by a single moon;
the source of the Yellow River is truly difficult to find. When one’s own mind-mirror is clearly seen, it reflects the fundamental form of heaven and earth to their very depths.
Luo Luo, you who have realized the Bodhisattva’s precious instructions!
Alas! The Ultimate Way has fallen into ruin; the faculties of sentient beings are dull and obtuse. They do not seek the True Eye and remain mired in ignorance regarding True Suchness (*tathatā*).

They mistake the correct for the erroneous and sink to the very bottom of the abyss. Taking suffering for pleasure, they find it difficult to accomplish the Way. They do not revere the worthy and virtuous, nor do they associate with them...
Superior friends debate the high and the low, contending over me and others. Those who study the Way have mouths but no hearts; those who recite the sutras commit nine errors for every ten words.

Though they bear the names of the teachings, they remain in a vast state of ignorance, failing to awaken. When they finally gain some slight insight through diligent inquiry, their deluded views prove difficult to eliminate.
I observe the times with alarm and am pained at heart in secret.

If there is one who practices truly and diligently seeks the True Dharma, taking self-nature as the fundamental principle in every thought and making Amitābha the master in every moment—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; eating or dressing;
from the mind reaching the mouth, or from the ears entering the heart—the divine mystery is inexhaustible and wondrous light manifests spontaneously. From this light, the Buddha appears. The light...

Born from the Buddha, light and light are perfectly interfused; in every thought-moment, there is quiescence. This quiescence is not that which can quiet, and this thought is not that which is thought.
A single piece of numinous mechanism manifests as reflections throughout the ten directions. Within sound is the self-nature; within the nature there is no sound.

Outside of sound there is no sound; outside of the nature there is no nature. The light of the nature encompasses the world; the radiance of light is the profound stillness of the Mind-school. All things are empty; the mind...
The mind is the Buddha. One Buddha is one mind; one mind is one Buddha. "One" pervades from antiquity to the present.
"One" is formless and signless. "One" is not merely one. "One" is precisely that which is one. To depart from one and attain one; to attain one and depart from one.

Departing from one is emptiness; attaining one is not emptiness. That which is not empty possesses form; that which possesses form is not empty. When both emptiness and existence are forgotten, it is wondrous.
Within this, there is realization; within this, there is comprehension. This meaning is inexhaustible. Who among men has awakened to its wondrous depths?

This single point of awakening and clarity leads one back to the Pure Land. Hehe! In the past I was muddled; now I have attained thorough enlightenment. When asked about my hometown, the bright path flows vast and wide.
Lotus flowers bloom in countless layers. To welcome my fellow practitioners: from Saṃsāra to Sukhāvatī is but a single step.
A single drop of this universally purifying nectar of bestowal—abide, abide, abide! Throughout the lands of the ten directions, all beings dwell in the cultivation of humanity.
What I now decree at this altar is entirely the merit of transforming the worthy into the sage; it is the wondrous elixir, the excellent remedy for liberation from suffering.
You all must each exert yourselves.
The Precious Teachings of the Tathāgata Saddharmaprabhāsa of the Past:
Homage to Amitābha Buddha. May they be heard by the faculty of the ear with utter purity and clarity;
may every word be distinct, illuminating sincerity, continuous and dense. By attaining the dual emptiness of mind and Buddha, it is naturally like the moon reflected in a thousand rivers.

Reflections appear when a mirror is bright; when the reflections depart, the mirror is empty. This is the true exposition of Buddha-recollection (*buddhānusmṛti*). Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down;

while eating or dressing; amidst both favorable and adverse circumstances; and throughout the constant changes of heat and cold—do not forget this for even a single moment. Your own mind is itself the Pure Land.
The Pure Land exists right within your own mind. There is nothing that is not Amitābha; there is nowhere that is not the Pure Land.

Although separated by ten quadrillion Buddha-lands, one arrives at the Lotus Pond in the snap of a finger. What is most to be feared are the afflictions of the mind and the heart of violence and slaughter.
A mind of pride; a mind of deceitful lust; a mind of mocking laughter; a mind of ignorance; a mind of stubborn attachment; a mind of greedy longing; a mind of fond attachment;
a mind of jealousy; a mind of negligence; and a mind of self-centeredness. A mind of indolence—all these are things that those who cultivate pure karma must most strictly avoid.
You all should act according to this; do not stray onto wrong paths. This Dharma gate is from our Buddha.

Compassion! This opens the unsurpassed, most supreme, and foremost expedient means—skillful, perfect, and sudden; easy to practice and easy to realize. In this degenerate age, the faculties of sentient beings are dull;
to study the Way through other gates is perilous and most difficult. To cultivate the Pure Land, one need only embrace these four characters of the True Mantra.
It is like Mount Sumeru: if you can rely upon it with absolute stability, it is like the sevenfold seas of fragrant water.
Thoroughly purifying it, there is a single point of numinous awareness. One illuminates this oneself; this numinous awareness is perfectly interfused.

Because it is a provisional name, it is provisionally named; being a provisional name, it is called "emptiness. It is neither empty nor provisional—the wondrous lies within. The six sense faculties are eternally pure.
The three delusions are naturally cleared away; from the level, pristine ground, one subtly gathers purity. He who is perfectly integrated cuts through everything with every stroke of his blade.
I have no further instructions to give. Withdrawing.
This is titled "The Precious Instructions of Tathāgata Munwang."
A single string of *muni* beads rests in the hand; the power of Amitābha Buddha is infinite.

May every person seize this moment to seek the way home; every lotus flower shares the same fragrance. When the entanglements are severed, one is Avalokiteśvara; with no going and no coming, the mind is sovereign.
The true essence is perfectly integrated as wondrous enlightenment; even the world of atoms turns its form into gold. The four teachings were originally...

The single principle is pervasive; though the stages of shallow and deep do not coincide, once one returns to the source and realizes the nature of true emptiness, one is a lotus-blossoming elder of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
With banners, streamers, and jeweled canopies shading the great trichiliocosm, every pearl is flawless.

Within each pearl, the three thousand worlds are contained; pearl meeting pearl is the way of the man of the Path. Zen meditation and the recitation of the Buddha’s name are fundamentally the same—transverse [and vertical] paths are one.

Though vertical distinctions differ, the single Dharma permeates all; the light of the hundred-and-eight wisdoms harmonizes mind and speech. When the ear-roots are illuminated, the mirror-light merges.
How many households are there from the southern neighbor to the northern neighbor? Having lost the Way of True Suchness, they wander further astray.

All are mired in delusion, difficult to awaken; clouds and mist fill the heavens as rain sprays sand. The sound of sutras and the chanting of Buddha-names call out to the deluded, yet iron chains sink into the river waves.
Rolling up the mud: Even if the Compassionate Ferry arrives to deliver all universally, how many people can ascend the green-cloud ladder?
Because during past kalpas I shared a karmic connection with you for the Pure Land, I have come here to guide and instruct you.
Having cultivated pure karma, one must be sincere. Cast aside worldly vanity and take refuge with a single mind to accomplish the Way.
Do you understand even a single word? From stillness arises reverence; from reverence comes oneness; and through oneness, one attains deathlessness.
From death one comes to life; from life, one returns to death. From death one reaches quiescence; from quiescence, non-existence. From non-existence, existence arises again.
When one reaches this stage of cultivation, it is simply the "One Character. This is the sequential progression; strive in this!

With a clear and penetrating wisdom, by reciting a single invocation of the Buddha’s name according to the precious instructions of the Tathāgata Vairocana, one can cause all myriad anxieties to become empty. The karmic obstructions of a thousand lifetimes are loosened in a single morning.
Wealth and status are but a dream of yellow millet; why not transcend the world with carefree ease? One will naturally attain high realization and primordial penetration. Even a fish in distress...
One may be transformed into a dragon; by all means, do not let your own mind waver. How tragic! The triple world is a cage, like a burning house.
If for a single thought one errs even slightly, ten thousand forms immediately manifest. It is like a boat without a rudder; when will it reach that shore of the Way?

Although the four thousand eight hundred Dharma gates may be practiced, they necessarily require the accumulation of merit and practice over many lifetimes and the endurance of bitter hardships before achievement is attained.
Only the single gate of the Pure Land—by exclusively holding the Name—purifies the three karmas; the land is purified through mindfulness, and the Buddha is realized through mindfulness.
To be reborn there in accordance with one's mindfulness is the most direct path. It requires only that one give rise to a sincere mind.
With faith, diligent and earnest cultivation, one swiftly transcends birth and death.

All kinsmen and sentient beings of the six realms of existence attain liberation in great numbers through the sound and light of my mindfulness of the Buddha. Is this not an extremely vast Dharma-gate?

Furthermore, this single aspect of mindfulness of the Buddha requires no expenditure of wealth or goods and involves no arduous toil; if practiced for a long time until it becomes proficient, it will be integrated into a single whole. By oneself—
There is great efficacy in this. It is a pity that while many people hear of its cultivation, those who resolve to attain rebirth are few.
Their accumulated karma fills the heavens, yet they willingly accept their retribution. Even if there were a demonic leader to preach verses, they would mostly be the openings of external paths.
I have now come here to universally exhort the people of the world: if you can firmly rely upon even a single phrase of Amitābha, you will surely be liberated from suffering.
An excellent method. Although the physical form remains in this eastern land, the spirit and mind are already in the Lotus Pond.
You disciples, wandering through the cycle of the six realms and mired in the five desires, are like a precious mirror covered in dust or gold left abandoned upon the ground.

You must rely upon the single phrase of Amitābha, practicing it morning and night with diligent effort to remove these obstructive defilements. If you do not slacken for a long time, they will naturally be purified and cleared away. Mind!
The light shines through. Although one remains amidst worldly conditions, those conditions do not defile them; the cause for rebirth in the Pure Land is thus assured.
Once disciples realize that the three realms are like a house on fire, they must resolutely and courageously recite the Buddha’s name to leap out of the fiery pit.

Having realized that Sukhāvatī is their true homeland, they must seek the Buddha’s compassion to be born upon the other shore. To cultivate the practices of purity, one must strictly refrain from killing. In this world...

Human habits form a prevailing wind; with hearts hardened by resentment, they kill one another. They respond to one another in a chaotic clamor, each asserting superiority over the other. How painful this is!
Mingwen, you who have come forward, since you have cultivated the skillful means of the True Dharma, you must sweep away all mundane thoughts.
Simply replace them with a single thought of Amitābha, and naturally all myriad anxieties will be cleared away and the dusty mind completely purified. Mingzhou, you who have come forward...
Those who cultivate pure karma must not indulge in excessive sleep, lest they waste their time. If one can awaken in a single morning, this is called the great accomplishment of pure karma.
Otherwise, one will ultimately attain rebirth while still carrying karmic residue. Strive with diligence! You who have come to reach the source:
those who practice the Way must sweep and cleanse their own minds; then, naturally, it will become bright and luminous, penetrating through to the ultimate.
The depths are clear and limpid; looking through both within and without, there is complete non-obstruction. Once again you see your former host of years ago.
You have been practicing for several years, O man from the Land of Pines, yet your turbid energy has not yet cleared. I offer you this verse: "The mind is level as water, the ears are like the deaf;
The eyes are fixed, the spirit concentrated, and even thought is empty. When emptiness reaches the very heart of emptiness, there is still the Buddha; The Buddha comes, and the Buddha goes."
The Buddha is emptiness and further emptiness; understand this subtly. Jingyuan has come forward; your pure merit is somewhat good.
However, there are stages of priority and sequence in practicing the Way: from the mind of equanimity to the four minds of emptiness; from the four minds of emptiness to the mind of cessation.
From the mind of quiescent cessation, one reaches the mind of spiritual subtlety; from the mind of spiritual subtlety, one reaches the mind of lucidity;
from the mind of lucidity, one reaches the mind of vast lucidity. If one’s pure merit can reach this stage, the level of rebirth will surely be high.
I grant you this verse: "The emotional shackles of attachment are severed in a single day; if you wish to attain pure stillness, let the four precepts be as they are.
Once you have reached the state of empty clarity through purification, the original nature of suchness will remain as it is.

Jing Cheng, when you previously gave rise to the fire of anger, it was highly incompatible with practicing the Way. Anger and the Buddha are two divergent paths: the Buddha is water, while anger is fire.
This most severely burns the forest of merit. You should silently recite the name of Amitābha from time to time; your mind will naturally become pure. Your remaining years are not many;
you must quickly leap out of this net—it is your great fortune. Pure precepts have come forward;

you are the master of this place of practice (*dharma-śālā*), skillful at leading the assembly and tireless in your efforts. As the good fruit is about to be realized, why need you worry so much? *Rao rao* (circumambulate)! White!
The clouds follow their will in this samādhi; flying geese ascend the lotus pedestal. You who have cultivated your resolve have come forward; I have descended to this site of practice.

It is both a cause for joy and a cause for lamentation. It is a cause for joy because those who cultivate [the path] have encountered the True Dharma and maintain right mindfulness, such that they shall later be able to realize rebirth in the Lotus Land.
It is a cause for lamentation because, although sentient beings hear the True Dharma, they are unwilling to apply earnest and sincere effort.
Indeed, how can one achieve liberation after death? I observe that among the disciples of this Dharma hall, those who are diligent are few, while those who are lax and negligent are many.
They vainly seek the title of "Dharma practitioner," their outward appearance being true while their inner spirit is false.

Little do they realize that these two characters, "Dharma" and "practitioner," offer no defense against the judgment of Old King Yama. Yet a single phrase of Amitābha can eliminate the karmic obstacles of ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes.
It serves as the causal condition for the four debts of gratitude and the three realms of existence. You practitioners who cultivate these paths are all observed by divine spirits.
Those who are diligent shall have their names inscribed upon the filaments of the lotus; the lotus will naturally become radiant.

At the time of death, the Bodhisattvas will come to welcome you, leading the consciousness of those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha and placing it within the lotus—what is known as the "Lotus."
Regarding the taking of conception in a womb: those who are indolent and lax find their lotus withered; after a long time, it dries up and perishes.
At the moment of death, one still receives retribution according to one's karma. I exhort you disciples here to maintain right mindfulness and meditative concentration;

you must cease all attachment to this Sahā world, which brings boundless suffering and binds one to enmity for ten thousand generations. You should instead give rise to a mind of fierce and courageous diligence, focusing—
Cultivate a single practice; quickly abandon the path of exhaustion and ascend to the sacred realm.

Jingxi, you have come forward; your sincere heart of compassion for the world remains unknown to no one. It is not that you lack effort; you must know that whether there is a karmic affinity for the Buddha or not, there is always a fixed basis for it.
From now on, every night bow in prostration toward the west and recite: "The Great Radiance... as follows:
Bring one string of prayer beads. Then request forty-eight strings of beads for Amitābha Buddha. Once again, sit cross-legged in silent meditation upon the Buddha for two incense sticks.
Continue in this manner for three years; thus, you shall attain one realization after another. Maintain this good and constant resolve; by all means, do not fall back or regress.
Pure Body has come forward. You, as the master of this place of practice (*dōjō*), must ensure that all matters are harmonious. Reciting the Buddha’s name (*nienfo*) originally values stillness;
yet, if you become attached solely to the state of stillness, you will fail to maintain mastery whenever you encounter conditions of movement. This is a grave illness of spiritual cultivation.
You must maintain mastery amidst movement, for it is even easier to gain strength in stillness. When movement and stillness are unified, [the Way] manifests of itself.
There is no longer the affliction of "two poles" lacking effort. As you have cultivated practice previously, you are a leader among the female assembly;

you must firmly embrace the single phrase "Buddha" and not allow it to waver. Recite until the waters of the Three Rivers are thoroughly clarified to the bottom, so that above and below are permeated by a single breath.
With every inhalation and exhalation, silently keep Amitābha in mind. When your practice reaches the state of absolute purity, [the realization will arise] of its own accord.
Yet, the single moon reflects in a thousand rivers, and the void hangs a precious mirror. As you approach the pure lotus, you must practice the pure karma;

you must regard worldly attachments as light. For every fraction by which worldly attachments are lightened, for that same fraction your karmic obstructions will dissolve, and for that same fraction your numinous awareness will be revealed.
In all matters, take integrity and luminosity as primary; purity is best. If you can truly [apply this to] one...
This is the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name to the point where one reaches the state of "not reciting while naturally reciting. It is like the effortless rolling of a chariot wheel.

When the power of purification reaches this stage, one may recite the name of Amitābha several hundred thousand times day and night; even while sleeping peacefully in one's bedding, the recitation continues as before.

At that time, all forms of greed, anger, ignorance, and attachment, as well as various discursive thoughts, will not arise. Why worry that the Way cannot be realized or that phenomena cannot be seen as empty?
This matter is already accomplished through single-mindedness; yet, within the state of principle-based single-mindedness (*li-yixin*), one must still apply diligent effort.

If you can directly take this up and maintain single-minded recitation, you will naturally reach the realm of principle-based single-mindedness. Do not lose this opportunity for a thousand [lifetimes].
This is the True Dharma rarely encountered in this age; exert yourselves! Jingjue, when practicing the Way in the future, you must advance slowly.
Busyness is of no use. If one sows a peck in spring, one may reap ten thousand bushels in autumn.

When the light of the mind of a practitioner wavers, they will inevitably encounter demonic afflictions. Jingzhu, when coming forward, you shall assist this Dharma center as the assembly gathers at the altar for the incense offering.
The kitchen staff prepares the meals, resulting in daily routines that cannot be made uniform.

Hereafter, whether reciting while sitting or reclining, with joy or with affliction, at high pitch or low, while walking or standing, in the *lianzhu* (rosary) style, according to one’s thoughts, during busy times or quiet times, or as *vajra-holding* recitation—you must follow my instructions and never lose the focus of your mindfulness. Upon reaching...

In the evening, before the Buddha, perform your daily devotions. Dedicate the merit to the four debts of gratitude, the three realms of existence, and all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, to adorn the pure lands.

Recite the Verse of Dedication once and prostrate three times. If you do this throughout your life without fail, it will ensure that at the moment of death you will depart for the Western Paradise with composure, unentangled by resentment or transgression.
I grant you these four lines for your awakening. *Heart-Mind* (Citta) (Note: The final line "賜爾四句悟之心" translates to "I grant you these four lines for your awakening of the mind-heart.")
Pure karma naturally dissipates. As karma dissolves, the mind becomes even more tranquil. By what power can one reach this state? It relies entirely upon the power of Amitābha.
Practice with diligent perseverance. Coming from within, coming forward; maintain single-minded persistence, and all external conditions will be stilled. Keep the heart upright and impartial.
The Great Way is impartial. Pure compassion approaches. During that night, sit in the lotus posture and silently recite the Heart Sūtra one hundred times.
Once again, settle yourself and burn a single stick of incense. When the hour of Jiazi arrives, lie down to sleep with your robes on. Rise at the fifth watch.

When your daily practice is completed as usual, disperse for meditation and walking practice. During the day, recite the Buddha’s name twenty thousand times and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* twenty scrolls, without ceasing in either winter or summer.
After six years, you will naturally find a place where you gain mastery. I grant you this verse: Where the golden light gathers, the jade platter is empty;
Within the signless and soundless Dharma-realm, What thing is there within the Dharma-realm that sees? You must know.
This object ○ proves fundamental penetration. Pure and direct, it comes forward.

Generally speaking, when the light of the eyes of worldly people falls upon the earth, the deeds they have performed throughout their lives are not necessarily entirely good or beautiful. The enmities and transgressions from beginningless time come forward to disturb them;

at that moment, when the jaw-joints fail to function, one relies entirely upon the Mind-King. That Mind-King is not something achieved in the present, but is truly forged through constant cultivation in ordinary times.
The karmic obstacles accumulated over ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes are difficult to overcome in battle; if the mind cannot reveal them, one is separated by the power of karma.
Even if a Buddha were to appear, there would be nothing that could be done. Would one not fall back into the dark paths?

Even if there were great virtuous ones in the world who acted as the eight classes of spirits and deities, it would ultimately be difficult to escape the suffering of saṃsāra. One must necessarily merge the light of the mind with the light of the Buddha into one.
A Fragment. It is certain that one may transcend this life. When Pure Buddha arrives, you shall establish a site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

Through the light and sound of the name of the Buddha, those in the ten directions and the seven realms of existence will be reborn in the immeasurable bliss of Sukhāvatī. Now your fame spreads throughout the ten directions, and humans and devas alike receive your grace.

Though the site of practice is small, when the multitude of hearts form a fortress, one who practices with diligence in this Sahā world will naturally attain a high station upon reaching the Western Land.
To transcend these stages, one must establish firm vows while yet alive. These should be like walls of bronze and pillars of iron, such that even ten thousand oxen could not drag them back.
Only then can one fearlessly withstand the gnawing of insects.

If you cannot practice wall-contemplation and asceticism, employing the long-term power of purification to sever karmic habits, you will ultimately have to rely on Amitābha’s compassionate vow to attain rebirth with your karmic burdens still intact; once you arrive there...

To cultivate and practice on the shore, one must also awaken to and clarify one's original nature; only then will the flowers bloom and one behold the Buddha. In the Sahā world, it is difficult to practice but easy to realize;
in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, it is easy to practice but difficult to realize. Strive diligently!

In the assembly of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, the Bodhisattvas’ precious instructions are for sentient beings who are all dull-witted and blind. The four characters of Amitābha are the unsurpassed medicine.
If one can awaken and break through them, one will be called a Great Awakened One within the ocean of wisdom. This is I, Master Puming. Ha ha! Human life is like a dream.
The substance of illusions is not solid; wealth, nobility, and splendor last but a hundred years.

Though one may hold high office and illustrious rank, have descendants as fragrant as cinnamon and orchid, possess white jade and gold, or dwell in lofty halls and grand mansions, once impermanence arrives, one will suffer ten thousandfold.
When one's allotted lifespan has ended, death leads to non-existence; how much more so for those in life who greedily seek nourishment for their bellies, committing manifold acts of killing?
By using the flesh of others to sustain one’s own body, one binds deep-seated enmity that will result in retribution. The suffering of this Sahā world can truly be called extreme.

If you wish to escape this suffering, no matter what thousands of methods or hundreds of schemes you employ, it is difficult to find peace through evasion. Through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, how could [this cycle] ever end?
One escapes [retribution]. Those with even slight knowledge who cultivate the ten wholesome deeds may avoid retribution for a time;

yet when their merit is exhausted, they must undergo the cycle of rebirth—how can they ensure that their true spirit does not perish? Once the true spirit has perished, they fall into inverted delusion and once again commit various evil karmas.
As retribution cycles on, there is still no end in sight. If one wishes to become an immortal, though one practices for billions of eons, it is difficult [to succeed].
If one attains accomplishment as an individual, one may perhaps become an immortal (*ṛṣi*), yet in the end, one cannot escape the suffering of sinking into the cycle of rebirth.
If you seek another path to the ultimate height, a gateway of skillful means, it is that which was proclaimed from the golden mouth of Śākyamuni Tathāgata:
there is a world in the West named Sukhāvatī; in that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha, whose power of vows is vast, immeasurable, and boundless.
In that land, there are forty-eight vows adorning the pure realm. Therein are ponds made of the seven treasures, filled with water of eight virtues.
The lotuses are of nine grades; the pavilions, towers, palaces, and halls, as well as the flowing waters, flowers, and trees, are all able to proclaim the sounds of the Dharma.

There are no female bodies, nor are there the three evil realms. If sentient beings of the ten directions wholeheartedly believe and accept [this teaching], and pay respectful homage morning and evening, reciting [the name]...

If you recite the Buddha’s name with single-mindedness and without distraction, at the time of death you will certainly be received by the Buddha and attain birth in that land, where you shall enjoy immeasurable and inexhaustible bliss.

Why do sentient beings not prepare for this supreme and most secure path sooner, so as to enter the Lotus Land and immediately ascend to the stage of non-retrogression? When you perform your fixed daily recitations, it should be as follows:

The Buddha treads upon golden lotuses. Listen to me as I recite the Buddha’s name; listen to me as I repent. If one practices this for a long time, the mind will naturally become pure and delusive thoughts will not arise.
The Pure Buddhas will come forward. Hereafter, within the *daochang*, perform the Universal Buddha Recitation (*pǔfó*) for seven days each season.
Every day, chant the Buddha’s name for twelve periods of incense-burning and recite the *Amitābha Sūtra* twelve scrolls. This is called the "Prison" [practice].
Great Confession of Emptiness. Pure Buddha, you delight in sitting in stillness and reciting the Buddha’s name. I now tell you: first, food and drink must not be excessive;
if one sits cross-legged for too long, the breath will not flow freely and the mind will find it difficult to concentrate.

Second, after sitting for a long time, one should perform walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) according to the prescribed rules to move the body, thereby harmonizing and circulating the blood vessels. If one suddenly leaps up abruptly before the blood vessels have been opened, illness will ensue.

It is difficult to cure. The third stage is when the Buddha has already been attained through silent realization and has reached full maturity; at this point, one must arise and walk about, yet remain vigilant to maintain the state.
One must not allow the fire of anger to stir. Only then can the Buddha within one's mindfulness continue uninterrupted day and night. Should it be severed even once, [the practice is lost].
To restore it to its original perfection is extremely difficult; it cannot be achieved as usual without redoubling one's efforts. As the ancients said: "Serenity with alertness is correct;
serenity with dullness is not. Alertness with serenity is correct; alertness with discursive thought is not. If serenity persists for too long, dullness arises;
if alertness persists for too long, discursive thoughts arise. Should you experience even a moment of unease, immediately go before the Buddha to repent. Next...

At night, sit again and recite again. After a long time, you will become proficient; right mindfulness will be unshakable. A single Buddha will stand before your chest, and all myriad conditions will be stilled.
You may fear encountering demons, but if your right mindfulness remains unshakable, the demons will naturally not enter your luminous mind.
The Precious Instructions of Chan Master Fuhu of the Great Ming’s Lotus Pond:
Cultivating the Way is by no means an easy matter. Having cast aside life and death, one’s mind is already extinguished;

let him be tempered by a hundred occupations and a thousand demons, yet if he maintains a single thought with steadfastness, he shall never turn back. Reading sutras, reciting the Buddha’s name, and practicing Zen meditation all rely upon sincerity of heart and action.
With full strength, he evaded a series of demonic words and obstacles; naturally, the solitary carp leapt toward the heavens.

Recalling years past when he first established the Dharma-hall, his cultivation of both vows and practice was far too hurried. Although today he has realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), he still sighs that the karmic retributions of the three miserable realms are long-lasting.
He searched minutely for the source of the ocean of nature; that single spiritual essence is ultimately not invaded by dust. Formless.
The signless encompasses heaven and earth; profound stillness and eternal clarity transcend past and present. The Great Way can be sought through single-minded sincerity;

through cessation and contemplation, concentration and wisdom, one moves the divine intelligence. What need is there for the Tathāgata’s true reality to be so wordy? Within the gate of honesty, walk with steady steps.

Within the manifestation of light, practice with the ears; let the ten thousand conditions of the one, three, and thirty-one cease. Transcending mind, transcending thought, and simultaneously transcending consciousness—go gladly to borrow a pillow from the Yellow Emperor (Xuanyuan).
When the recollecting mind and the Buddha-mind are both absent, there is no Buddha and no mind;

mind and Buddha are together. That which is the Buddha is the mind, and that which is the mind is the Buddha. Recollect the mind and recollect the Buddha, and the Buddha-light unfolds. When there is no recollecting mind...
"In this very thought, at this moment, both mind and Buddha are empty; their circular radiance intermingles, originally devoid of substance.

This is the Elder of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. I am indeed Master Lianchi. Ha ha! I have gone to the worlds of the East to transform and guide those with whom I share a karmic affinity to return to my Buddha-dharma.
You all, open the spirit-writing board; I have come here to this site of practice to enlighten and transform."
In Jambudvīpa, the most evil of lands, there are sentient beings who undertake such virtuous deeds; this is truly difficult to find. Pure Buddhas have come before you.
You must universally exhort all with whom you have karmic ties in this Sahā world; you should advance with fierce courage and must not be indolent.
Your practice of the *fangsheng* (releasing life) assembly is likewise a virtuous thought; however, if you merely use ordinary wealth, how can it provide universal salvation? [The womb...]

Those born from eggs, moisture, or transformation—their numinous awareness is no different and no distinct from that of the Buddhas. It is only because their created karma is exceedingly deep that they receive this retribution.
When the retribution is exhausted, yet residual karma remains unexhausted, they continue to undergo karmic retribution in the netherworld.

Although my Buddha-dharma is vast and compassionate in its salvation, it delivers only those who are delivered; as for those who create [karma] again, they come back. By noon, the hells are only just emptied, and by the hour of *wei*, [they are full once more].
At that time, the hells will again be filled. Therefore, you must perform the Universal Buddha Seven-Day Rite at every seasonal change in the Dharma-assembly.
This is called the "Repentance for Releasing Living Beings and Attaining Liberation. In past kalpas, when I manifested in the body of a high-ranking official, I practiced this merit;
I now proclaim it for you. This is a great fortune for all of you, and a great fortune for immeasurable and boundless sentient beings.

The Dharma transmission of the Jewel-like Instructions of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva has reached the Eastern Land for nearly a thousand years. Though he repeatedly and earnestly exhorted those with karmic affinity, it is regrettable that true faith among worldly people is scarce;

how then could they dwell in peace and nourishment upon the golden lotus? May the wisdom of the Dharma altar and the Buddha’s light merge as one, and may we cultivate both aspiration and practice together.
How vast! Alas, I lament that those of my Lotus Land are truly my own kin; how can they be submerged within the waves of karma? How tragic!
Both the paths of celestial beings and immortals are but pavilions within an illusion; in the end, one cannot avoid the five signs of decline.

Although the human realm possesses the stubborn blessings of a firefly, these are nothing but deep pits for creating karma; ultimately, it is difficult to escape falling back down. As for the asuras, they cling to their own...
Yes. How could one attain clarity and penetration into the Great Way? In the three evil realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, hunger is compounded by punishments—how painful!
Distracted by the dust of the mundane world, one ultimately becomes a fish in a cauldron; blinded by a hundred errors, one is instead like a bird in a cage.
How can this compare to the Lotus Land of Ultimate Bliss, where one wanders at ease and with freedom, free from both cold and heat throughout the four seasons?

In this world of springtime, one walks upon the precious ground and sits cross-legged upon golden steps. One should quickly awaken to the original source and repent for the karmic obstructions accumulated over many lifetimes.
One must directly accept the truth and ensure that this life does not pass in vain. The True Dharma abides in the world as briefly as a flash of lightning or a spark from flint;
yet, because the conditions of sentient beings have now ripened, they will believe and follow when exhorted. For a Bodhisattva has descended to the world in the West.
Sometimes manifesting in the form of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, officials, or lay devotees, they point out the way through the ford of delusion.
Once the conditions for rebirth have been fully assembled, they act as guides; immediately thereafter, they abandon this physical body of blood and flesh and depart.

Thereafter, those people should recite the name with a voice that is both full and slow. When reading the sutras, each phrase must be clearly articulated; only then can sentient beings of the heavenly realms [attain their goal].
You have understood clearly. Jingfo has come forward. Within your monastery, add seven days of Universal Buddha (Pufu) services each season to deliver your ancestors.
Reverent filial piety is the very foundation for attaining the Way. That your ancestors are delivered to higher rebirths is the greatest form of filial piety among all forms of filiality.
Add three days of Buddha assemblies each season to deliver those who have drowned. Hehe! This is your monastery.
The merits of your practice are complete. Whenever you encounter a period for repentance, first prepare the written petitions for cremation and purify the Buddha-altar.

You take delight in dhyāna-concentration; listen to my instructions. If you wish to sit in meditation while reciting the Buddha's name, you must place both knees together and keep them level and even.
Shake the body four or five times. With both hands, rub the eyes open and closed four or five times.
Slowly exhale turbid air from the mouth four or five times, then inhale pure air four or five times. Thereafter, concentrate the spirit.
In winter, one must wear thick clothing; in summer, thin clothing. The garments on the body must be loose and ample; the trousers, robes, and belts must be untied and relaxed, both above and below.
As you move back and forth, ensure that your breath is not obstructed. Sit with your body as straight as a mountain peak, without leaning against anything on any of the four sides.
Form the *Mida-in* (Amitābha mudrā) with both hands, keeping your knees and legs level and centered. Align your eyes with your nose, and your nose with your heart.
Following the inhalation and exhalation of the breath, silently recite the name of Amitābha. Begin for the duration of half an incense stick, gradually increasing to one or two incense sticks.
When one's practice reaches deep proficiency, the mind is no longer restless or agitated; there is only the four characters "A-mi-t'o Fo.
Beyond this, not a single trace of active movement remains. Even amidst thunderclaps, the thought-moment does not waver, resembling water without ripples.
When one reaches this stage of practice, it is simply a matter of ensuring that the mind of cultivation does not regress and that the power of meditative concentration becomes profound.

Then, the light of the mind will naturally manifest, and pure karma will easily be accomplished. At that time, yet another set of demonic realms will appear before one, layer upon layer, to refine the practitioner’s mental nature.
Generally speaking, when the Buddha transforms demons to come forth, the mind becomes exceptionally pure; when demons transform Buddhas to come forth, the mind remains cool and serene.
If you naturally become restless and agitated within, you must simply embrace the four-character mantra with firm resolve and recite it continuously.
Then you will know that even atop a hundred-foot pole there is room for further progress, and that throughout the worlds of the ten directions, one’s entire body is manifest.
